strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: amortizing repeated entropic optimal transport computations without requiring training examples from the target dataset. Combining adversarial sample generation, dual-potential prediction, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets is a well-motivated contribution.

The Hilbert projective loss naturally handles the scaling ambiguity of Sinkhorn potentials. Proposition 4.3 provides a sound pointwise residual-to-solution error bound for positive kernels, giving a mathematical rationale for bootstrapped targets.

The reported warm-start improvements are substantial within the tested setting. For example, Table 2 reports reaching 0.01 marginal constraint violation on CIFAR in 3 iterations, versus 17 for Gaussian initialization and 47 for initialization with ones. Four datasets, 500 samples per dataset, and five-run confidence intervals for convergence curves provide useful empirical evidence.

The manuscript supplies algorithm pseudocode, network architectures, training hyperparameters, computational budget, and a code link. The random-noise ablation also provides evidence that the learned generator contributes beyond synthetic training alone.
weaknesses: The central universality claim is unsupported for the implemented method. Theorem 4.1 assumes equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint, whereas the implementation uses a 392-dimensional latent for two 784-bin marginals and does not enforce that constraint. Moreover, generator coverage would not itself establish uniform predictor accuracy. Results on four image datasets demonstrate cross-dataset transfer, but do not establish reliable approximation for any pair of distributions, even at the stated fixed dimension and cost.

The evaluated objective is inconsistent across the manuscript. Algorithm 1 returns the transport cost <C, Gamma>, while Section 5.2 defines the reference value as the entropy-regularized objective <C, Gamma> - epsilon H(Gamma). These differ even at convergence. The paper must clarify which quantity is computed for both predictions and references; otherwise, the relative-error results and the claimed approximately 5% standalone-solver accuracy cannot be interpreted unambiguously.

The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is explicitly excluded based on an assertion that it fails out of distribution, without presenting that comparison. Evaluating its dual-objective training with comparable synthetic data and computational budget would help distinguish the benefits of the proposed loss and generator from those of broader training exposure. The claim of being the first meta neural OT solver also needs narrowing given the cited Meta Optimal Transport work.

Theorem 4.1 requires mathematical correction independently of its applicability. Even q(z) = ReLU(lambda z) is noninvertible and has an atom at zero, so the stated inverse and density formula cannot hold at every nonnegative point. An almost-everywhere statement on the strictly positive orthant is potentially repairable. Remark 4.2 also does not follow from closure under Lipschitz composition: composing rectified maps need not preserve full support.

The adversarial update needs stronger justification. Section 4.4 stops gradients through the entire target, including its dependence on the generated marginals. Consequently, generator ascent follows a frozen-target surrogate and need not increase the residual after recomputing that target. Proposition 4.3 bounds prediction error for a fixed instance; it does not establish that this update discovers difficult instances. A targeted ablation or analysis would strengthen the central adversarial-training argument.

The practical efficiency evidence remains incomplete. Figure 8 reports timing against initialization with ones but omits the stronger Gaussian baseline. Separate initialization latency, timing methodology, and the workload needed to amortize approximately 40 minutes of training are not established. Evaluation is also confined to one grid size, cost, and regularization value; controlled tests with concentrated or near-boundary marginals would better assess the claimed distributional breadth. These gaps limit the conclusions beyond the demonstrated warm-start gains.
